page: Microsoft Azure E16ds_v4 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance powered by Microsoft Hyper-V. The system is provisioned with 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 8 physical cores on an Intel Xeon 8272CL processor operating at a base frequency of 2.6 GHz. Built on the x86_64 architecture, the processor features 35 MB of L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets including AVX-512, AVX512_VNNI, AES, and FMA. Hardware acceleration is absent, with zero GPUs included.

Memory capacity is configured at 128.0 GB of RAM, yielding an allocation of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance comes equipped with 644 GB of direct-attached local SSD storage alongside support for Azure Premium Storage remote volumes. Benchmarks show uncached memory bandwidth sustained at 69.79 GB/sec for large-block reads and 41.6 GB/sec for writes, alongside cached read throughput reaching 830.49 GB/sec.

Benchmark evaluations reveal modest single-thread compute capabilities, placing in the lower quartile on both stress-ng and Geekbench single-core tests. Conversely, multi-threaded workloads operate squarely in the middle tier, evidenced by a multi-core Geekbench score of 6,410 and a PassMark CPU score of 15,834.08. In database tests, the instance records 13.72 million Redis SET operations per second and steady throughput across PassMark database operations.

The hardware configuration trades single-threaded peak compute for memory capacity and high local I/O density. Because of its 1:8 vCPU-to-memory ratio and bundled high-speed local disk, the E16ds_v4 provides practical cost efficiency for memory-intensive enterprise tasks without requiring over-provisioned compute cores. Appropriate deployment workloads include relational database servers, in-memory caching solutions like Redis, intermediate ETL processing, and medium-scale analytics applications requiring fast temporary storage.

The system provides 128.0 GB of system memory, maintaining an 8.0 GB per vCPU ratio, and includes 644 GB of local SSD temporary storage with no hardware GPUs. Benchmark testing reveals lower-tier single-core performance alongside balanced multi-threaded throughput, illustrated by a Geekbench multi-core score of 6,410 and 13.72 million Redis SET operations per second. The hardware layout is cost-efficient for applications prioritizing memory volume and local scratch disk over raw CPU frequency, making it suitable for relational databases, in-memory caches, data transformation jobs, and static web serving.
